intro: How Turkish is pronounced and how it works: the spelling rules and a key to the symbols in the pronunciations, then the grammar basics — vowel harmony, suffixes, the cases, possession, and the verbs.

sections.heading: About the pronunciations
text: Pronunciations follow standard Istanbul Turkish and are written as broad (slashed) IPA. Stress usually falls on the last syllable.

items.note: endings change their vowel to match the word: evler, kızlar

sections.heading: Symbols used in the pronunciations
sections.text: Each symbol that doesn't sound the way an English speaker might expect, with a word from the vocabulary that uses it.

items.note: open a, as in "father" but shorter
pure e, like "ay" in "say" without the glide
pure o, like "oh" without the glide
ee said with rounded lips (French u, German ü)
e said with rounded lips (German ö)
w (or a soft g) without rounding the lips
the sound before it is long

sections.heading: How Turkish grammar works
text: Turkish builds words by adding suffixes one after another, each with one job: ev (house) → evler (houses) → evlerim (my houses) → evlerimde (in my houses).
There is no grammatical gender (o means he, she and it) and no word for "the"; bir (one) works as "a".
The verb comes last: Ben kahve içiyorum. (I'm drinking coffee — literally "I coffee drinking-am"). Prepositions come after the noun, as postpositions: benim için (for me).
Two sound rules shape every suffix: vowel harmony chooses the suffix's vowel, and some consonants change at the joins.

sections.heading: Vowel harmony
sections.text: A suffix's vowel copies the last vowel of the word. Suffixes come in two patterns: two-way (e or a) and four-way (i, ı, ü or u).

table.note: Some loanwords break the pattern, and a few suffixes never change (-ken, -yor, -ki).

sections.heading: Consonant changes
text: After the voiceless consonants f, s, t, k, ç, ş, h, p, a suffix starting with d or c switches to t or ç: evde (in the house) but kitapta (in the book); geldi (came) but gitti (went).

At the end of many words, p, ç, t and k soften to b, c, d and ğ before a suffix starting with a vowel: kitap → kitabı, ağaç → ağacı, renk → rengi, çocuk → çocuğu. One-syllable words usually don't change: top → topu.

When two vowels would meet, a buffer letter goes between them: y in most suffixes (araba → arabaya, to the car), s for 'his, her, its' (araba → arabası), n before case endings after that (arabasında).

sections.heading: The cases
sections.text: Endings shown on ev (house) and okul (school). Each follows vowel harmony and the consonant rules above.

rows: Ev büyük. (The house is big.) Kitap okuyorum. (I'm reading [a] book.)
table.note: The accusative is the key difference from English: use it only when the object is specific. Bir kitap okudum. (I read a book.) Kitabı okudum. (I read the book.)

sections.heading: Plural
sections.text: Add -ler or -lar: ev → evler, kitap → kitaplar. After a number, the noun stays singular: iki kitap (two books), çok ev (many houses).

sections.heading: Possessive suffixes
sections.text: "My house" is ev + -im: evim. The pronoun (benim, my) is optional and adds emphasis.

sections.heading: Noun + noun: the possessive compound
text: Two nouns join with the possessive suffix on the second one: ev kapısı (house door), Türk kahvesi (Turkish coffee), otobüs durağı (bus stop).
With a specific owner, the first noun also takes the genitive: Ali'nin evi (Ali's house), evin kapısı (the door of the house).

table.note: Pronouns are often left out, since the verb ending shows the person: Geliyorum. (I'm coming.)

sections.heading: "To be": personal endings
sections.text: Turkish has no separate verb "to be" in the present. A suffix on the noun or adjective does the job.

table.note: Negative: değil + the ending: Yorgun değilim. (I'm not tired.)

sections.heading: var and yok: there is, to have
sections.text: var means "there is, exists" and yok "there isn't". With a possessive, they mean "have" and "don't have".

rows: I have a brother or sister.

sections.heading: Verbs: the basic form
text: The dictionary form ends in -mek or -mak: gelmek (to come), yapmak (to do). Drop it to get the stem: gel-, yap-.
Tense, negation, question and person are added to the stem in a fixed order: gel + me + di + m = gelmedim (I didn't come).

sections.heading: Present continuous: -iyor
sections.text: The most-used present tense: what you're doing now or these days. Add -(i)yor (the vowel follows the four-way harmony) and the personal ending.

table.note: A stem ending in a vowel drops it: beklemek → bekliyorum (I'm waiting), anlamak → anlıyorum (I understand).
-di becomes -ti after a voiceless consonant (gitti). A second past, -miş, reports something you didn't see yourself: Gelmiş. (Apparently he came.)

sections.heading: Future and the simple present
text: Future: -(y)ecek / -(y)acak: geleceğim (I will come), yapacaksın (you will do), gelmeyecek (he won't come).

Simple present (aorist): -r, -ir, -ar for habits, general truths and offers: Her gün kahve içerim. (I drink coffee every day.) Yardım ederim. (I'll help.) Its negative is -mez / -maz: içmem (I don't drink), içmez (he doesn't drink).

sections.heading: Questions
text: Yes-no questions use the particle mi (mı, mü, mu), written as a separate word after the word being asked about; the personal ending attaches to it: Geliyor musun? (Are you coming?) Türk müsün? (Are you Turkish?)
Question words: ne (what), kim (who), nerede (where), nereye (where to), nereden (from where), ne zaman (when), neden / niye (why), nasıl (how), kaç (how many), ne kadar (how much).

sections.heading: Postpositions
sections.text: Words like "for" and "with" come after the noun.

rows: eve kadar (as far as the house)
